key_insight: EEG foundation-model performance for clinical decoding is highly sensitive to dataset identity, split strategy, and negative controls, and can be outperformed by classical features or even random initialisation on some tasks.
clinical_relevance: Clinicians and researchers should be cautious when interpreting pretrained EEG model gains, because apparent improvements may not generalise across patient-disjoint settings or different datasets.
method: Benchmarked 6 EEG foundation models on 5 clinical tasks across 4 datasets
Used frozen linear probes with leave-one-subject-out, subject-grouped, and recording-level splits
Ran targeted controls: random initialisation, random features, label permutation, scrambled-label fine-tuning, and projection sensitivity
evidence_signal: Dataset identity was decoded almost perfectly from frozen embeddings (AUROC 1.000 at PCA-50), while Korean dementia diagnosis from the same pipeline was near chance (0.528), and a randomly initialised encoder sometimes beat pretrained REVE.
watch_item: Results may not reflect real-world deployment if evaluation is not patient-disjoint and if strong classical baselines and negative controls are not included.
paper_title: Stress-Testing EEG Foundation Models for Clinical Decoding: Dataset Identity and Targeted Negative Controls
